vectors.enisa_quote: Adversaries obtaining information on the orientation of the satellite
vectors.reason: ENISA names what is learnt, not where the attacker acts; orientation is radiated in housekeeping telemetry on the TT&C downlink, so a receiver outside the mission is the best-supported origin. Ground-side optical/radar observation and proximity observation are not modelled.

rows.enisa_quote: Adversaries obtaining information on the orientation of the satellite
rows.sparta_quote: The attacker records spacecraft-to-ground traffic, real-time telemetry
rows.reason: Orientation is carried in downlinked housekeeping telemetry, so recording the downlink is how the attacker obtains it.

rows.sparta_quote: captures mission traffic in transit, on ground networks or over the space link
rows.reason: Generic capture of mission traffic over the space link is the step the downlink-specific capture builds on; the uplink half of it is not what yields orientation.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may field their own ground system, transportable or fixed, to transmit and receive mission-compatible signals
rows.reason: A rogue ground station is the outside receiver in view of the satellite that picks up the telemetry downlink.
Link band, modulation and framing must be known to demodulate the telemetry that carries orientation.
Passive eavesdropping is the capture setup; its output is the telemetry stream.
Harvesting housekeeping and ancillary downlink channels is where attitude and mode information is read.
The receiving station (antenna, LNA, demodulator) is the equipment needed to hear the downlink.
Disabling fault management is deactivation of safeguards (TR50), not learning orientation.
Disrupting or deceiving the downlink hides activity from operators; it does not give the attacker information.
Jamming is link denial (TR44).
Inhibiting spacecraft functions is a denial effect, not information gathering.
Obfuscating on-board values conceals activity from monitors; ENISA's attacker reads, not hides.
Altering the command-counter value hides commanding; it reveals nothing about attitude.
Altering the rejected-command counter hides failed attempts, not orientation.
Faking received signal strength conceals link activity; not information gathering.
Tampering with receiver lock modes is evasion on the command path.
Changing telemetry downlink modes alters what is sent; the threat reads what is sent.
Switching crypto modes to hide traffic is evasion; no orientation information results.
Evasion by clock manipulation conceals activity, not a reading of orientation.
A spoofed ephemeris corrupts on-board position knowledge; ENISA's attacker learns the satellite's state, not falsifies it.
Masquerading is impersonation (TR43).
Subverting protections in safe mode enables commanding; orientation is learnt passively.
Rootkit evasion hides malware on board; no malware is described here.
Concealment and decoys defend a satellite; here the attacker is the observer.
Hiding behind space weather is a concealment tactic and not information gathering.
Replay sends commands; the threat only observes.
Replaying commands is an active step with no passive orientation gain.
Replaying bus traffic acts inside the spacecraft.
Geofence-conditioned execution is a trigger on board, unrelated to observation.
Bypassing encryption defeats protection of the link (TR45); ENISA says nothing about encryption here.
A single-event upset is a fault-induction effect on board.
A rootkit is injected software (TR46).
Exploiting reduced safe-mode protection is a commanding aid.
Editing routing tables modifies on-board data; the threat reads information.
Editing the clock modifies values on board.
Valid commands used to flood the satellite are the denial-of-service of TR40.
Erroneous input is a flood/confusion attack, not an observation.
Spoofing is forgery of signals (TR54).
Forging time is a forgery attack and gives the attacker no orientation data.
Spoofing bus traffic acts on board.
GNSS-like spoofing is forgery of signals (TR54).
Jamming is link denial (TR44).
Uplink jamming is link denial (TR44).
Downlink jamming is link denial (TR44).
GNSS jamming blinds a receiver on the satellite or user side; it does not reveal orientation.
Replay-driven exfiltration induces new transmissions by commanding; here passive reading of existing telemetry suffices.
Traffic analysis exposes link patterns and node power, not orientation; the orientation data is inside the telemetry content.
Timing attacks infer secrets from response latency, which is not attitude data.
Intercepting the uplink collects commands, not the orientation carried by telemetry; ENISA TR29 holds uplink interception.
An out-of-band covert link moves data off the spacecraft (TR38); the attacker here only receives what is already sent.
Reconfiguring the spacecraft to emit data on new paths is TR38's exfiltration.
Reconfiguring a transponder to forward traffic is exfiltration by reconfiguration (TR38).
A payload channel used for data extraction follows an implant (TR46).
Software supply-chain insertion is TR55.
Supply-chain insertion plants code before flight; no code is involved in ENISA's observer.
Poisoned build tools are not related to passive observation.
Hardware tampering at manufacture is not described by ENISA TR33.
Compromising the SDR is an access path that ENISA does not describe.
A compromised neighbour is an access path to another satellite; orientation is read from the downlink, not from a neighbour.
A backup-channel foothold is for commanding.
Backup ground-station compromise is a commanding foothold.
The backup receiver is a commanding path.
Rendezvous gives physical vantage; ENISA gives no nearby-platform text and the rf_link path suffices for orientation in telemetry.
Emanation analysis infers keys and counters, not orientation.
A docked vehicle is a physical access path not described here.
Grappling is a physical attack, not observation of orientation.
The hosted-RAN door is an access path that ENISA does not name.
Update-pipeline compromise is software implant (TR46).
Commanding the spacecraft is control seizure (TR52).
The generic rogue entity is covered by its child IA-0008.01, the rogue ground station that receives telemetry.
A rogue spacecraft as observer is the proximity case; ENISA names no nearby platform.
An ASAT weapon destroys, not observes.
A trusted relationship is an access path into systems, not the radio observation of telemetry.
Collaborator access is an access path, not a reception.
Vendor access is an access path, not a reception.
The user segment is a springboard to mission cores, not an observer of telemetry.
Safe-mode access is a commanding technique.
Auxiliary device compromise is an on-board access path.
ATLO compromise is pre-flight and not related to learning orientation.
Host-spacecraft compromise is a pivot from hosted functions.
Abusing native functionality changes the spacecraft; here it is only read.
Timing manipulation changes the spacecraft; ENISA names no change.
Compromising ground systems is the ground origin's entry; ENISA TR33 names no ground foothold, and telemetry is read off the radio link.
Commanding mode changes is TR28.
Configuration manipulation is parameter modification (TR57).
Altering data is TR39; here only confidentiality is lost.
Command flow manipulation is TR32's subject.
Changing software/firmware is TR42.
Resource exhaustion is denial of service (TR51).
Pivoting from a hosted payload is a movement step, absent in an observer.
Exploiting bus segregation is lateral movement, absent in the threat.
Hopping across crosslinks moves control, but ENISA describes learning orientation.
Rideshare-payload pivots are not described.
Replacing keys cements control; the attacker here reads.
Renting commercial ground-station time is an alternative to owning one; RD-0001.01 is the kept preparation.
Obtaining keys prepares decryption, which ENISA does not describe.
Generic capability staging prepares exploits.
Staging an upload exploit prepares commanding.
Cryptographic-algorithm discovery prepares decryption, not observation of attitude.
Commanding details prepare command injection.
Scanning for payload, user and crosslink channels widens the target; orientation telemetry rides the TT&C downlink.
Credentials are for authenticated access, not passive reception.
Capturing the command path yields commands; orientation is in the downlink.
Active scanning transmits probes; ENISA's attacker only obtains information.
Monitoring safe-mode indicators supports timing of commanding.
